match.reason: The closest bank point, leg-separation-powers-2, teaches the same idea but at senior Legal Studies depth, with Governor-General, responsible government and the overlap of executive and legislative power, which is more than a Stage 5 Commerce point needs, so the change in depth is too large for an adaptation.

draft.title: The separation of powers
card: The separation of powers splits government power into three parts. This stops any one person or group from holding all of it.
Legislature
parliament, which makes and changes laws.
Executive
the Prime Minister, ministers and government departments, who carry out the laws and run the country day to day.
Judiciary
the courts, which apply the laws and settle disputes about them.
draft.remember: Three parts share power: parliament makes laws, the executive carries them out, the courts apply them.

a.q: A government department begins running a new program that parliament has passed into law. Which part of government is it acting as?
opts: The executive, because it carries out a law
The legislature, because it works with a law
The judiciary, because it follows a law
The legislature, because it set up the program
a.why: Carrying out laws and running the country day to day is the job of the executive. The legislature makes laws, so a department running a program that is already law is not doing that.
a.clue: Who makes the law, and who puts it into action?

b.q: A court in Perth hears a dispute about a business contract and decides what the law means for both sides. Why does this show the separation of powers at work?
opts: Courts apply the law, separate from the lawmakers
Courts make the law, separate from the lawmakers
Courts carry out the law, separate from the lawmakers
Courts run the country, separate from the lawmakers
b.why: The court applies the law to a dispute. This is the job of the judiciary, which is separate from the parliament that makes laws and the executive that carries them out. The tempting option says courts make the law, but that is the job of parliament.
b.clue: Which of the three parts settles disputes about the law?

a.best: The executive, because it carries out a law

b.best: Courts apply the law, separate from the lawmakers

problems.detail: Why (b) says making law is the job of parliament, not the courts. Australian courts also make common law through precedent, which students may meet in Commerce law topics. The why could say parliament is the main lawmaker, rather than implying courts never make law.
